hook.text: Every model in a dbt project now has one more reader: a language model, behind an ask-your-data assistant. It reads the same tables and definitions an analyst does, but it takes them literally, and it answers thousands of questions nobody reviews.

plan.text: Six questions on making that safe, and on knowing when it isn't. Five are worked through, and one quick one comes last.

t2s.text: Question one. Why does text-to-SQL over raw tables give confident wrong answers?
t2s.spoken: Question one. Why does text-to-sequel over raw tables give confident wrong answers?

t2s-hard.text: Because the hard part of a business question isn't the SQL. It's the definitions the SQL has to encode.
t2s-hard.spoken: Because the hard part of a business question isn't the sequel. It's the definitions the sequel has to encode.

t2s-guess.text: Ask for revenue, and an assistant writing SQL against raw tables has to guess. Net of refunds? Cancelled orders? Test accounts? Which of three similar tables, which join path, and does it fan out?
t2s-guess.spoken: Ask for revenue, and an assistant writing sequel against raw tables has to guess. Net of refunds? Cancelled orders? Test accounts? Which of three similar tables, which join path, and does it fan out?

t2s-rows.text: Here are eight orders from five customers, and one customer is a test account.

t2s-run.text: Sum every order: fourteen hundred fifty dollars. Only the completed ones: eleven hundred ninety. Completed, and not from the test account: four hundred forty.

t2s-valid.text: Each guess is a valid query with a plausible number, and the biggest is more than three times the smallest. Nothing in the SQL would look wrong to the person who asked.
t2s-valid.spoken: Each guess is a valid query with a plausible number, and the biggest is more than three times the smallest. Nothing in the sequel would look wrong to the person who asked.

t2s-name.text: That's the failure to name: not an error, but a fluent, plausible, wrong number.

t2s-past.text: [slowly] And no query can find the right one in the rows.

sem.text: Question two. What does a semantic layer change for an AI assistant? It moves the definitions out of the guess and into code.

sem-declared.text: Metrics, their filters, the dimensions they can be sliced by, and the join paths between entities are declared once.

sem-job.text: The assistant's job shrinks from writing SQL to choosing: a metric, dimensions, filters and a time grain. The layer compiles the SQL.
sem-job.spoken: The assistant's job shrinks from writing sequel to choosing: a metric, dimensions, filters and a time grain. The layer compiles the sequel.

sem-same.text: Ask for net revenue, and the assistant, the dashboards and the finance report all get four hundred forty, computed the same way.

sem-fail.text: And a question the layer doesn't model returns an error saying no metric matches, not an invented query. A refusal is far cheaper than a wrong number in a board deck.

sem-active.text: So if an executive asks for active users last week, and nobody has defined active, the right answer says so, and offers the closest governed metrics, or an exploratory query labeled as unverified.

sem-drift.text: Having the language model define it on the spot is metric drift by design: its version won't match the dashboards or finance.

sem-trade.text: The price is coverage: the assistant can only answer what's been modeled. So many teams route modeled questions through the layer, and fall back to text-to-SQL, clearly labeled, for exploratory ones.
sem-trade.spoken: The price is coverage: the assistant can only answer what's been modeled. So many teams route modeled questions through the layer, and fall back to text-to-sequel, clearly labeled, for exploratory ones.

ready.text: Question three. What makes a dbt project AI-ready? Everything that helps a new analyst helps an assistant, with less tolerance for gaps, because an assistant won't ask.

ready-desc.text: Describe every public model and column, including the grain, one row per order, and how to use it: for revenue, the net revenue metric.

ready-tests.text: Test what the descriptions claim: the key unique and not null, relationships for foreign keys, and accepted values, so the assistant knows the real statuses are completed, refunded and cancelled.

ready-access.text: Grant the assistant's warehouse role the public marts only. Marking staging models private stops other models building on them, not queries.

ready-rest.text: Put every number the business argues about in the semantic layer. And check source freshness, so an answer can say as of when, and the assistant can refuse to answer from stale data.

ready-input.text: Drop the words and test accounts from the end of this description, and an assistant writing its own SQL from it reports eleven hundred ninety.
ready-input.spoken: Drop the words and test accounts from the end of this description, and an assistant writing its own sequel from it reports eleven hundred ninety.

ready-review.text: So if an assistant drafts the descriptions from the SQL, review them like code.
ready-review.spoken: So if an assistant drafts the descriptions from the sequel, review them like code.

eval.text: Question four. How do you evaluate a natural-language analytics assistant? With a golden set: real questions from the people who'll use it, each with an answer you've verified.

eval-mix.text: Mix easy lookups, multi-step comparisons and ambiguous phrasings.

eval-store.text: Store the verified result, not only a reference query, because many different queries are correct.

eval-run.text: Here are three answers to one question: what was net revenue? The first is the reference. The second uses a different join and different aliases, and also returns four hundred forty. The third runs without an error, and returns eleven hundred ninety.

eval-score.text: Compare the query text, and the second, which is right, fails. Count whatever runs, and the third, which is wrong, passes. Compare result sets, which is called execution accuracy, and both are scored correctly.

eval-decline.text: Include questions it should decline: metrics nobody has modeled, data the user may not see, and nonsense. Measure how often it refuses those as carefully as accuracy on the rest.

eval-slice.text: Slice the scores by difficulty and domain, because an average hides the category that fails every time.

eval-regress.text: Then run the set as a regression suite on every change to the models, the semantic layer, the prompt or the language model, and grow it from the production questions that went wrong.

review.text: Question five. How do you review a dbt model an assistant wrote? With the checklist you'd use for a junior colleague, aimed at what assistants tend to get wrong.

review-grain.text: Grain: what is one row, and is there a unique test proving it?

review-refs.text: References: ref and source, never a hard-coded schema name, which breaks in another environment and hides the lineage.

review-incr.text: Incremental logic: a lookback window in the filter, so late rows are caught, and a unique key, so a rerun updates rows instead of duplicating them.

review-pair.text: The two only work as a pair. Here, one order arrives late, dated two days before the newest row loaded.

review-dup.text: Duplication: does this number already exist under another name? Assistants are good at writing a second, slightly different revenue, like completed orders at eleven hundred ninety, next to the governed four hundred forty.

review-tests.text: And tests and docs come with the model, including a test that would fail without the change.

r-connect.text: Question six. How do AI assistants connect to the warehouse and to governed metrics? Through the interfaces dashboard tools use: a semantic layer API that takes metric and dimension names, and catalog metadata for discovery. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is a common way to expose them, and dbt Labs publishes an MCP server.

r-connect-design.text: Run the assistant as the user, with that user's row and column permissions, never as a superuser. Give it read-only credentials and limits on cost and time, since it writes an expensive cross join as easily as a cheap lookup. And log every question, query and result, for audit and for the golden set.

close.text: Under every round in this series sit two questions: what does one row mean, and what does this number mean? An assistant can't decide either. It can only read what you wrote down, and it reads it literally.

close-practice.text: That closes the series. Every topic page has concept checks, three have challenges that run in the browser, and a bank of a hundred and ten multiple-choice questions covers the whole track.

ready-access-why.text: That removes the wrong choice, rather than hoping it makes the right one.

t2s-decision.text: Which reading counts as revenue is a company decision, so it has to be written down where the assistant reads it.

ready-caution.text: One caution: documentation is now an input.

review-strict.text: A filter for dates after the newest one loaded misses it.

review-look.text: A three-day lookback catches it, but reads three orders it already loaded, and without a unique key appends them a second time: ten rows for seven orders. With the key, seven.

eval-luck.text: One catch: a wrong query can match by luck. Without the test account's orders, the third returns four hundred forty too, so test on data where the readings differ.
